title: Albuquerque: Jay McShann and the Gray brothers teach him to write
summary: At Silver's Resort in Albuquerque he meets Henry and Hunter Gray and Jay McShann, who teaches him changes so he can write parts, modelled on Earl Hines tunes heard on the radio; he also recalls hearing the Blue Devils.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I stayed there for a while. And then J.R. went back to Wewoka. We went right to Wewoka then. He got a gig going out to... He went to a town in New Mexico...Albuquerque.
You went to Albuquerque.

We went to Albuquerque to play. I had met these two guys there, Henry Gray and Hunter Gray, and Jay McShann. But I knew Jay from Muskogee, but I hadn't known the two Gray brothers. So they were out there with a band called...
What did they play?

One played trumpet and one played tenor. So they were out there playing with Jay McShann, and they went to Albuquerque. They were working at a place called Silver's Resort. And the guy that owned the thing was a state commissioner.
Silver's Resort?

Yeah, Silver's Resort. J.R. got the gig out there to replace them. So when I got out there, I saw these guys, and I knew these guys could play, you know, because I had heard them play in Shawnee, Oklahoma one night in a dance, and I'd heard the Gray Brothers, and I know that Jay can play -- so I wanted to be with him. So I told him. He said, 'Well, we got another job we're going on to, so why don't you come on and go with us.'
In the meantime, Watts had me and a guitar and a drum and himself, and I said, 'Well, I can't learn anything just the way they're playing, because I was teaching them' -- because I'm there. It's better I go where I can learn something, and I want to know... I asked Jay would he teach me how to write for the group, so he said 'Yeah.' So we had two trumpets and a tenor and a bass and drums and a singer; he had Bill Powell. So I learned a whole lot from Jay, like all the tunes Earl Hines was playing -- 'Deep Forest' and what was that, 'Bubbling Over'... I don't know whether you know anything about them tunes.
'Deep Forest' I remember.
Yeah, that was his theme song, 'Deep Forest.'
Yeah, right. 'Bubbling Over'?
Yeah. [SINGS 16 BARS] But I wrote that out for the band...
You used to hear these bands on the radio, I guess. You could hear...
Yeah, we could hear Earl Hines and so forth on the radio.
Were you buying records then, too? Did you have records?
No, I didn't have no records.
You didn't have records.
No. We didn't have nothin' to play it on in the first place.
So what kind of a model would you use when you started to do your writing, when you first started to write?

Whatever I heard, I could write. I just had to... Like, Jay taught me the changes on the piano. So I would figure that out, and then I'd write out the instruments for trumpet and tenor. They're all in the same key, so it was easy for me to write them. So I wrote out the trumpet parts and the tenor parts for Henry. It was real easy to do. But without Jay McShann, I don't know what would have happened, because he taught me the changes to most of the tunes that I was trying to write. And I learned all of them, like the tune "I Wished On The Moon" and a
couple more tunes that I remember, if I can think of the name of them -- but that's kind of hard to do, to think of them now.
Had you heard other bands like the Blue Devils by then?

Oh yeah, I heard the Blue Devils in Oklahoma City. They came down there and played a dance, and they sounded pretty nice. But I really didn't know that much about music, so I couldn't say that they were good or that they were...
But you remember hearing them when you were in Oklahoma City.
Oh yeah, yeah. Then my brother, Ben, came through there...
Ben Johnson.
Yeah, with T. Holder. I had heard about him, but I never heard him play -- but I didn't think so much of him, come to think of it.
When was this? Was this in Albuquerque?
No, this is in Oklahoma City.
Oh, back in Oklahoma City.
